turns.zh: 对啊。我想再提一个我们录制前讨论过的建议，我觉得这对大家可能有帮助。虽然方向有点偏，但我还是想确保提一下，那就是Shreyas Doshi关于利用杠杆效应的观点。我知道你对这方面思考很多。他提了些非常好的建议，如果大家想深入了解如何作为产品经理找到最高杠杆机会，我们会给出那期节目的链接。你能给那些没听过这建议的人分享一下吗？

turns.speaker: Mayur Kamat
turns.en: This is true for no matter what level of career you are in, but you have a finite amount of time and largely you have more problems than you have time to solve them. The question is which ones you work on. And this becomes even harder, let's say you're a CPO now because all of them are important, otherwise they will not come to you in the first place. The question is, which one do you work on? And the principle is simple. You work on problems that have a 10X positive or a negative impact. I mean the number can be 10, 5, 300, depending on finance it would be a hundred, some companies might be three. And in most FinTech companies one of two problems, it's a growth problem or a compliance problem because both of them can have a negative or positive 10X impact and that's what you focus on. That's what you spend bulk of your time. What was interesting for me, my first executive roles, that was Google, I was a product manager. (01:08:01): I joined what was White Pages back then as a VP of product. I was my first kind of... And White Pages, Alex Allgood, Seattle, founding legend, three companies, all unicorns now. Incredible, very good personal friend and mentor. What was truly interesting when I joined it, they're like, "Okay, this is your desk, this is the product area. So we had two offices, this is when everybody worked in office five days a week." And I'm like, "Okay, where does Alex sit?" And he's like, "Oh, he's sitting with accounting." And I'm like, I didn't think about it because I thought his office is near accounting. Then I find out he doesn't have office, he has a floating desk. So all the other desks were fixed, but he had a movable desk and he would move his desk to one of the departments, which I think had the highest leverage opportunity. And he would sit there at that desk when that department till that either problem was solved or the opportunity was realized, and then he would literally move his desk and then go to product or tech or finance. (01:09:08): And that was his way of... You could literally visualize him working on the highest leverage problem by his desk moving. And then that combines that with what we talked before about details and a little bit, I think I didn't mention it about the humility that you need to have to be working in the detail. A lot of the times, especially later in your career, you're like, hey, this is beyond me. This is below me. Why do I need to do that? I have so many PMs or data analysts or somebody should do it. Why would I do it? And that was kind of again, just a quick story there. I remember we were trying to figure out our growth channels and we found out that, hey, we are kind of really tapping out on paid, on social, on referrals, but SEO was something we just hadn't worked on for a while. We're building a caller ID app and what we wanted to do was when somebody types a phone number in Google, we want to be the first link to say, hey, is this a spam call or not? (01:10:10): Or whose number it is. And if we could then we could get them to download our app. That was the hypothesis. So I present at the executive team meeting to Alex, like, "Hey, I have a team. I want to hire a product manager focused purely on SEO and because I think that's one of our highest leverage areas right now." And Alex is like, "Hey, the whole White Pages, I built based on SEO. People who type people's name and the first thing used to be a White Pages link. I'm one of the best people in the world to work on SEO." I'm like, "Yeah. So?" He's like, "Let me run this product." I'm like, "Okay, what do you mean?" He's like, "No, no, I will be the product manager for this for however long you need it." I'm like, "How's [inaudible 01:10:54]?" (01:10:54): "They don't worry about it. Just tell me about the engineers." So again, he moved his desk to where that product team sat, and for the next three months he was the product manager on that scrum. So he would come to my product team meetings, give us update on what's happening with the SEO scrum, and then an hour later I would be in the leadership meeting giving my update to him, and truly he was operating it saying, this is high leverage area for the company, high leverage for my yards. It should be high leverage for me. I'm the best person to do it. I'm going to be in the details and do it. CZ, same at Binance, there were a lot of products that he would just sit on himself. There were very few people at Binance who would say no to CZ, but one of my lead PMs who worked on the products that CZ worked on, he would tell them no all the time. (01:11:41): They would just baffle all the other executives, how is he saying no to CZ and none of us are doing it? Hey, that was his product area that CZ was working on, and there was that mutual respect there that, hey, we know this thing and he is going to say no to me because probably not a good idea. So that humility and attention to detail is required to work on the high leverage problems. A lot of the high leverage problems are not, as I said, not strategy decisions. They're not language markets to go after and stuff. A lot of them are like, why is this thing not working as well as it needs to be? And a lot of time the devil is in the details and you need to be over there. I think combining that, knowing what is high leverage or not, and two, both having the humility and the patience to be able to go dig deeper and solve that. (01:12:34): Some of them are quick ones. Like if I'm looking today at, let's say how many of our signed up users convert into a long-term monthly daily active user, that could be something I focus on for a month. Because we're running a lot of experiments on early onboarding screens, early rewards, early incentives, early loyalty program, and at some point it might be like, oh, the team's got it. I've given all my... What I could do there. It's functioning. We have great PMs. I trust their execution on this. Let me just go focus on some of the compliance challenges that we have or fraud issues that we have in France. (01:13:13): Those kind of being able to kind of... The only way that works for me is I keep a very three calendar because you cannot do this without that. If you have hundreds of meetings, hundreds of one-on-ones daily standards, a lot of recurring meetings, you just can't find time to go work on high leverage problems. So that would be my kind of other stuff is you should have plenty of open spaces on your calendar. A full calendar is a badge of shame, not a badge of honor.
turns.zh:
无论你处于职业生涯的哪个阶段，这都是千真万确的。但你的时间有限，面对的问题远远多于你能解决的时间。关键在于你要选择优先处理哪些问题。当你身处高管职位时，这份挑战会倍增——毕竟所有问题都至关重要，否则它们根本不会找上门来。问题在于，你该专注于哪个领域？原则很简单：选择能带来10倍正面或负面影响的问题。具体数字可能为10、5、300，金融领域可能需要100个，某些公司甚至只需3个。在多数金融科技公司中，要么是增长问题，要么是合规问题，因为这两者都能带来10倍的正面或负面影响，这才是你应当聚焦的方向。这也是你投入精力最多的领域。

对我而言，最初的管理角色是在谷歌担任产品经理。（01:08:01）我加入当时名为White Pages的公司时，担任产品副总裁。这是我职业生涯的首个高管职位。在西雅图，亚历克斯·奥尔古德（Alex Allgood）是传奇人物，曾创立三家公司，全部成为独角兽企业。令人惊叹的是，他对我极为友善，是我的人生导师。

加入White Pages后，他们对我说：“这是你的办公桌，负责产品领域。”当时公司有两个办公地点，员工每周五天在办公室办公。我问：“亚历克斯的办公桌在哪？”他回答：“他和财务部门坐在一起。”我很惊讶，因为我以为他的办公室就在附近。结果发现他根本没有固定办公桌，而是随处移动。所有固定办公桌都固定在某个部门，而他会根据项目需求灵活调整办公地点。遇到需要解决的难题或抓住机遇时，他就会转移办公地点，随后再返回产品、技术或财务部门。

（01:09:08）这就是他专注于最高效问题的秘诀——通过办公桌的移动轨迹清晰可见。结合之前讨论的细节，我还想提及高管需要具备的谦逊态度。尤其在职业生涯后期，人们常会说：“这超出我的能力范围。”“这不值我亲自操刀。”“我有太多产品经理、数据分析师，应该让他们去处理。”这种心态必须克服。

记得我们曾研究增长渠道时，发现付费推广、社交媒体和推荐渠道都已触顶，而SEO却被忽视。我们开发的来电识别应用希望当用户在谷歌输入号码时，能第一时间显示“该号码是否为骚扰电话？”并显示号码归属信息，从而引导下载应用。这就是我们的假设。

我向亚历克斯汇报时说：“我组建团队，专注SEO。”他反问：“整个White Pages都是基于SEO打造的。用户输入名字时，最先显示的链接就是White Pages。我是SEO领域的专家。”我回应：“是啊，那又怎样？”他说：“让我负责这个产品。”我问：“什么意思？”
他说：“不，不，我会担任这个项目的经理，直到你需要我为止。” 我说：“[01:10:54的部分不清]？” （01:10:54）：“他们对此并不担心。只管跟我说说工程师的情况。” 于是，他再次把办公桌搬到那个产品团队所在的位置，接下来的三个月里，他一直担任那个Scrum项目的项目经理。他会参加我的产品团队会议，向我们汇报SEO Scrum项目的最新进展，然后一个小时后，我又会在领导会议上向他汇报情况。他真正在运作这个项目，称这是公司的高杠杆领域，也是我部门的高杠杆领域。对我来说也应该是高杠杆领域。我是做这件事的最佳人选。我会深入细节去处理。  
在币安，CZ也是如此。有很多产品他会亲自负责。在币安，很少有人敢对CZ说“不”，但我手下一位负责CZ所负责产品的首席产品经理，却总是不停地说“不”。（01:11:41）：这让其他高管很困惑，如何对CZ说“不”，而我们其他人都不这么做？ 嘿，那是CZ负责的产品领域，我们之间有一种默契尊重，知道这件事我们需要深入研究，可能不是个好主意。所以，要处理高杠杆问题，需要具备谦逊和专注于细节的态度。很多高杠杆问题并非战略决策，不是要进军哪个语言市场之类的。很多时候都是，某个功能为何没有达到应有的效果？很多时候，关键就在细节里，需要亲自去深挖。我认为，要结合两点：一是知道什么是高杠杆问题，二是具备谦逊和耐心，深入研究并解决问题。  
（01:12:34）：有些问题很快就能解决。比如今天我关注的，比如我们的注册用户中有多少转化为长期月活跃用户，这就是我未来一个月要关注的重点。因为我们在早期入门界面、早期奖励、早期激励、早期忠诚计划上做了大量实验，到了某个阶段，可能团队已经掌握了诀窍。我能做的已经做完了，现在运行良好。我们有优秀的产品经理，我信任他们的执行能力，那我就去处理法国市场合规挑战或欺诈问题吧。  
（01:13:13）：要做到这点，我会保持一个非常清晰的日程安排，因为没有日程安排根本不行。每天要开数百个会议、数百次一对一沟通，还有很多重复性会议，你根本找不到时间去处理高杠杆问题。所以，另一个关键点是日程要留有充足的空闲时间。满满的日程安排是耻辱的象征，而不是荣誉的象征。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: These are awesome stories. Just the metaphor of the moving desk is so good. That's the epitome of a... Like what you're describing is what people now call founder mode, where the founder just goes in the details working on the problem. Brian Chesky actually did this at Airbnb while I was there. He took on a new product and was like mini CEO, essentially. I don't know if he'd called himself the product manager 'cause I don't think he loved product managers. He kind of famously got rid of product managers, which he didn't actually... But yeah, he did that very much and he sat with the team, kind of created a whole space for the team that he was in. These are awesome stories and really good example of a founder using their power to unblock and finding the highest leverage opportunities. (01:14:29): To kind of start to close off our conversation, I'm going to take you to a couple recurring themes on this podcast, recurring segments on this podcast. First, we're going to visit AI Corner and in AI Corner I ask, what's a way that you have found to use AI in AI tool, a bunch of AI tools in your work to work more efficiently to work to create better quality work?
turns.zh:
这些故事太棒了。光是那张移动的书桌这个比喻就特别妙。这简直就是……你所描述的这种状态，就是人们现在所说的"创始人模式"——创始人会深入细节去解决问题。布莱恩·切斯基在我任职Airbnb期间就这么做过。他接手一个新产品时，简直就是个迷你CEO。我不确定他是否自称产品经理，因为他对产品经理不太感冒。他还曾以强势手段裁掉了产品经理团队，但后来又反悔了……不过他确实亲力亲为，与团队同坐一室，为团队开辟出专属空间。这些故事太精彩了，也是创始人如何运用权力破除阻碍、寻找高杠杆机会的绝佳范例。

（01:14:29）  
在结束今天的对话前，我想回顾一下本播客的两个常驻板块。首先，我们将探访"AI角"。在这个环节中，我会问大家：在工作中，你们是如何利用AI工具来提高效率、提升工作质量的？

turns.speaker: Mayur Kamat
turns.en: I still haven't found a game changer for me personally. Something that I use right now and I'm a little bit not-
turns.zh: 我个人还没找到那种能彻底改变局面的工具。就拿我现在用的那些AI工具来说，虽然还算能用，但总感觉……

turns.speaker: Mayur Kamat
turns.en: He was like, now I am a little bit not sure that am I not doing something right, what the other people are, or I'm a little bit too jaded for it. (01:15:10): So we have Gemini across the work. So for meeting notes and stuff, works great, especially for folks who don't make it. We use a tool called Writer for our copywriting and UX teams, especially because we are operating in Europe across several languages. So being able to generate that very quickly, especially for illustrations and in-app messages and stuff that's been a, several tools now. But Writer just has, the copywriting market is really well done over there. (01:15:43): If you ask me across N26. But even when we did this at Binance or at Agoda, there are three areas where AI is complete game changer. One is on coding. Again, you can use whatever latest tool for prototyping or not most value, especially for the companies I have worked at, which are fairly large companies, very large code bases. (01:16:09): Having some sort of co-pilot that's integrated with your repositories. Rough data, maybe somewhere between 18 to 25% productivity boost for a developer, which is fairly massive, right? So that's one category, game changer. Customer support, game changer. Whether we should do it at scale or not, that's a different kind of more ethical/human question to ask there. But for solving the bottom 70 percentile problems, "Why is my card declined? Why is there a hold on my account? What happened to the replacement card I shipped? Why is it not arrived?" Basic questions, AI automating now almost 60, 70% of that. Customers getting that real feedback. Game changer. (01:16:58): And the last one is just on fraud and being able to just understand patterns better on real customers versus not. At Binance, we had this product where users could exchange crypto with each other. I could pay you Bitcoin and get Thai bath in return, huge amount of fraud. (01:17:18): And they're using AI just to understand language patterns of fraudsters versus not fraudsters. Massive. So again, as a company level, there is an incredible set of advancements across these three areas: developer productivity, customer support, and fraud. But for me personally, I'm like, what would I use that suddenly makes me a better CPO? I'm still struggling a little bit over there, but I don't think we need something at that level because largely what still remains the domain of humans is decision making and taking the brunt of the impact of what decisions you make because I would love to blame AI for some of my bad decisions. That's not why [inaudible 01:18:10].
turns.zh: 他当时说："现在我有点不确定自己是否做错了什么，或者其他人是怎么做的，又或者是我太现实了吧。"（01:15:10）：所以我们在工作中使用了双子座（Gemini）平台。用于会议记录等事务效果很棒，尤其是对于那些不常到场的同事。我们为文案和用户体验团队使用了一个叫Writer的工具，尤其是因为我们在欧洲运营，涉及多种语言。所以能快速生成内容，特别是插图和应用内消息之类的，这对我们来说非常重要。（01:15:43）：如果让我谈谈N26的情况。但即使是在币安或Agoda做这件事时，人工智能能彻底改变游戏规则的三个领域之一。一个是编码领域。再次强调，你可以使用最新的原型工具，但最有价值的是，我曾工作的那些大公司，它们拥有庞大的代码库。（01:16:09）：拥有与你的代码仓库集成的某种协助工具。粗略数据显示，开发者的生产力可能提升18%至25%，这相当可观，对吧？所以这是一个能改变游戏规则的领域。客户支持也是如此。是否要大规模应用，这是一个更具伦理/人性化考量的问题。但对于解决底层70%的问题，比如"为什么我的卡被拒了？为什么我的账户被暂停了？我寄出的替换卡为什么还没到？"这些基本问题，人工智能现在能自动处理60%到70%的案例。客户能得到真实反馈。这又是一个改变游戏规则的领域。（01:16:58）：最后一个是反欺诈领域，能够更好地识别真实客户和欺诈者的行为模式。在币安，我们有过用户之间进行加密货币兑换的业务。我可以用比特币给你，然后换取泰铢，结果发现欺诈行为大量存在。（01:17:18）：他们利用人工智能分析欺诈者和非欺诈者的语言模式。这太重要了。所以从公司层面来看，在这三个领域——开发者生产力、客户支持和反欺诈——都有令人惊叹的进步。但对我个人而言，我在想，有什么能让我一下子成为更出色的首席产品官？我在这方面仍有困惑，但我觉得我们不需要那种级别的工具，因为决策权和承担决策后果的责任仍然属于人类。我倒是希望能把一些糟糕的决策归咎于人工智能，但这不是关键所在。[01:18:10未录音]

I remember when we had zip and it was a game changer, but there was a big file you needed to send over a slow network, so you compressed it and sent it and then expanded it. turns.zh: 是的，是的。但再说一次，我对此持乐观态度，不过总体来说我不太喜欢……我觉得这有点让人感到厌倦。现在你有一些工具，你只需写几句话，它们就能把它生成一篇长文。然后你还有一些工具，能把长文压缩成简短的文字。其实你本可以一开始就只说几句话，这样就能省去来回折腾的麻烦。这就像反向压缩文件。我记得以前我们用压缩文件时，它彻底改变了局面，但当时你需要把大文件通过慢速网络发送，所以先压缩再发送，最后再解压。而现在我们却反其道而行之。我们把小文件做大，再发送过去，然后别人又把它压缩小。但在以下三个领域，如果你所在的公司技术水平不高，如果没有出色的生产力提升工具，如果没有优秀的LLM机器人来分流客服工作，如果没有分析用户交易或沟通模式、识别欺诈的工具，那这些都是我首先会关注的重点。

turns.en: Yeah, so from the product side, my probably most spectacular failure was I was the first PM on Hangouts. And if you ask Nikhil, he'll probably say he was my boss then. It was an effort the size I've never seen before or after in my career. We had thousands of people working for me. We had entire power of Google. We had Larry literally sitting with us saying we can do anything we want Chrome to do. And we still didn't manage to build a great messaging product. (01:20:18): So when I look at pure product-sense, product decision-making was, there's several reasons now I'd had luxury of 15 years to analyze that on solving for the wrong audience, solving for the wrong DNA of the company. I have this premise that certain companies can never succeed at certain type of products like Microsoft with mobile or Google with social or Facebook with enterprise, it is just the DNA of the founder actively acts against you succeeding there. (01:20:54): I would've said Google with enterprise as well. But then Sundar came and Larry was no longer the CEO and that's when the enterprise took off. They literally had to change the CEO to win in certain segments, but more, and then again, I worked in Nagoda during COVID, so travel company during COVID, Binance during its probably most tumultuous area of compliance and government scrutiny. There's a lot of missteps there around externalities. I think one of the main kind of learnings from that is just don't take on projects that are going to be six months, a year, because you just generally don't have control over the macro. Things just move way more faster. And that's probably cemented my kind of now product philosophy of just doing small things very quickly, spending most of the times doing that. You still launch big products, but even over there we try and get early signals as soon as possible. But because in Nagoda, like one of the big projects we launched was we wanted to control the payments infrastructure for all the hotels and we thought if we had that device in the hotel's desk, so not only for bookings made online, but for everything that happens at the hotel, if we control that infrastructure, not only would we make money, but we had a touch point with the users that went beyond booking the travel. (01:22:29): Travel as you know, is not a high frequency activity. You book once, then you book six months later and most of the time people would not come to Nagoda, they would just go to Google and go to some other website. So we wanted that touch point that stayed with them and thought payments would be a great avenue to do that because that's something you do every day. And again, we did it in the Nagoda style. (01:22:51): So we did an experiment. We started very small and literally went to the mall and bought these $50 Android devices where we ran our software that people could just scan the credit card by a camera and charge it. It was incredible. We had thousands of hotels use it. And then COVID hits and then there's literally nobody going to hotels anymore. But it took us like six, nine months because of the licenses, and so to launch it. And in hindsight probably, I mean you couldn't have thought about COVID with that sense, but still the amount of time it took to launch the product was something we could have done better. So learnings for most of it is don't take too long to launch, don't take too long to validate your hypothesis.
turns.zh:
是的，从产品角度来看，我最失败的经历当属担任Hangouts项目的首位产品经理。要是问尼基尔，他很可能会说当时我是他的上司。这项工作规模之大，前所未见，亦后无来者。我手下有数千名员工，动用了谷歌的全部资源，拉里甚至亲自与我们开会，说我们可以随心所欲地复制Chrome的功能。然而，我们最终还是没能打造出成功的即时通讯产品。（01:20:18）从纯粹的产品视角来看，我现在回顾时，发现有几个关键失误：15年的职业生涯让我有机会剖析失败根源——无论是定位错误，还是与公司基因不符。我坚信某些公司注定无法在特定产品领域成功，比如微软在移动端、谷歌在社交领域、Facebook在企业级市场。这些公司的创始人基因本身就与成功背道而驰。

（01:20:54）我本以为谷歌在企业级市场也会遭遇同样的困境。但后来桑达尔上任，拉里不再担任CEO，企业级业务才得以腾飞。有些公司确实需要更换CEO才能在特定领域胜出，但这背后又有无数教训。比如我在新冠疫情期间负责Nagoda项目——一家旅行公司——而Binance则深陷合规与政府监管的风暴眼。这些外部因素导致的决策失误教会了我一个重要经验：别轻易接手需要六个月、一年才能完成的项目，因为宏观环境变幻莫测。即便项目推进顺利，也要尽早获取反馈。比如Nagoda团队曾想控制酒店支付基础设施——不仅监控在线预订，更要覆盖酒店内所有支付场景。我们以为通过掌控支付环节，能与用户建立超越预订的深度联系。但旅行本质上是低频行为，人们通常一次性预订，隔几个月才再次下单。因此我们选择从小处着手，先在商场测试50美元的安卓设备，内置支付扫码功能。效果惊人，数千家酒店采用了这项技术。但疫情来袭后，酒店行业陷入停滞。由于许可证问题，产品上线耗时六到九个月。回想起来，即便当时无法预见疫情，但上线延迟仍是可以避免的教训。因此关键在于：快速验证假设，缩短产品周期。
